title: Save Your Hardest Questions for Recruits
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short Admired Leadership piece reframes the hiring interview as more than a selection filter. It starts from the observation that most interview time is spent on candidates who are never hired, which looks like pure waste. The author's move is to turn that time into value by posing the organization's genuinely hardest, unresolved problems to candidates, stripped of confidential detail. Because recruits lack the insiders' blinders and assumptions, their responses both reveal their experience and judgment and occasionally surface a fresh insight or an approach the leader had not seen. The piece closes by arguing that every interview, including those with candidates who are not selected, can leave the leader with something useful.
points: Interviewing candidates who are ultimately not hired is framed as sunk time that leaders can recover by asking about real problems rather than rehearsed hypotheticals.
Posing the problems that genuinely keep a leader up at night tests a candidate's judgment and experience more honestly than standard competency questions.
Outsiders without the team's shared assumptions can occasionally offer an insight, or describe how others handled a similar problem, that exposes a leader's blind spot.
Even weak answers are diagnostic: the way a candidate approaches a big, context-poor problem tells the leader how talented they really are.
quotes: Sifting through prospective candidates, narrowing the list to finalists, and then interviewing to find the best match is arduous work. The significant time spent with the candidates that aren’t hired or selected is a huge waste of time.

Evaluating the potential skills, talent, and fit of prospective candidates is the mainstay of the interviewing process. Leaders who want to make the most of this experience and gain true insight into the candidate save their hardest problems for them.

Without giving away confidential information, the best leaders pose their most complex issues and problems to potential hires who don’t have the same blinders or work from the same assumptions. With fresh eyes, the recruits can tell you how they would go about addressing the issue or solving the problem. You might be surprised by what you learn.

To be fair, most candidates won’t have the context or insight to provide an answer of significance. But the question and response will tell you a lot about how experienced they are and what judgment they bring to a big problem. This is valuable information for assessing how talented they really are.
On occasion, a candidate will provide an answer that gets sparks flying. Perhaps it is not a solution, but an insight that gives you a new idea.
Saving your knottiest problems for recruits turns every interview into highly valuable time. Why go through the process and have nothing to show for it regarding those you don’t select?
